title: Three Names
context: Grade 5, the closing page on percentage. An adult sees three answer lines under each shape. What the page is doing is naming one amount three ways: a fraction, a decimal and a per cent, each read through hundredths. Any equivalent fraction is right unless lowest terms are asked, and the self-assessment and the words are the child's own.

writeup.why: Name a shaded part as a fraction, a decimal and a per cent, see all three as one amount, accept any equivalent fraction unless lowest terms are asked, start from a per cent, and say the chapter's words in the child's own terms.
writeup.look: A shape at the left, cut into equal parts and labelled Whole and 100%. The three name cards stand at its right, and on the last phase the word cards and the can-do cards.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Three Names' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many parts are shaded out of how many. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The shape stands inside a square 440 by 440 at x 110, y 230, labelled Whole and 100% above it: a bar of cells 440 long, a circle 440 across, or a square of small squares 440 on a side. Its parts are exactly equal, cut by near-black lines; shaded parts are deep blue and unshaded parts stay warm white. The Shape switch and the Parts buttons run in a row along y 690 from x 110, each labelled in words. The Fraction, Decimal and Per cent cards stand one above the other at x 640, y 240, x 640, y 360 and x 640, y 480, each 260 by 90 and labelled in words; they turn green together when all three name the shading. The Hundredths and Simplify buttons stand at x 940, y 240 and x 940, y 330, and when either works the words Both terms light vermilion over the Fraction card while the shading does not change. A grey 0 labelled Place holder appears on the Decimal card only where a zero holds a place open. On the fourth phase the word cards lie in a tray at x 110, y 230, their pictures stand at x 420, y 230, and the five can-do cards stand in a column at x 900, y 230, each with Yes, Almost and Not sure boxes. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a point key, a fraction bar key and a % key. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. The part the question gives, as shaded cells, a fraction, a decimal or an amount, is deep blue, labelled Given. The per cent, fraction or decimal the working reaches, and what is left after a part is used, is green, labelled Answer or Left. Both terms multiplied or divided by one number, and the times one hundred step before the % sign, are vermilion, labelled Both terms or Times 100. A unit fact that puts two amounts in one unit is violet, labelled Unit fact. The part used, taken away or not won is rose, labelled Used or Not won. The step, cell or number being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a decimal is grey, labelled Place holder, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded cell of a whole stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the % sign is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The shape shows the last shading, with its fraction, decimal and per cent in green beside it.

source_tool.description: A shape stands at the left of the working area, labelled Whole and 100%: a bar of equal cells, a circle cut into equal parts, or a square of equal small squares, picked on the Shape switch. Parts buttons cut it into 2, 4, 5, 10, 20, 25 or 50 equal parts, numbers that all go into 100. Tapping a part shades it deep blue, and tapping again clears it. Three cards stand to the right, labelled Fraction, Decimal and Per cent. A Hundredths button grows both terms of the fraction until the denominator is 100, lighting the words Both terms vermilion, and the decimal and per cent cards fill from those hundredths. A Simplify button divides both terms by their HCF, and the shading does not change. When all three cards name the shaded part they turn green together. Typing a per cent into the Per cent card shades that many hundredths of the shape. On the last phase three word cards, per cent, percentage and equivalent fractions, are dragged onto pictures, and five can-do cards are ticked Yes, Almost or Not sure by the child. A number pad types a fraction, a decimal or a per cent. The running count at the top left of the canvas is how many parts are shaded out of how many.
source_tool.art_direction: Shaded shapes on squared paper / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: hundred grids of ten rows and ten columns, strips cut into equal cells, fraction bars with their denominator of one hundred built beside them, measuring jugs, tapes and scales with their units written on them.

Every whole is drawn the same size as every other whole it is compared with, and its parts are exactly equal: a strip of ten has ten cells of one width, and a hundred grid is always a full ten by ten.
A whole is always labelled 100%, so the child sees what one hundred per cent means before any part is named.
Where shaded cells are counted, exactly the stated number is shaded, and they stay countable at a glance: full columns of ten first, then single cells.
A product that becomes a per cent is always written with its brackets, and the % sign comes last. A decimal reaches a per cent through its hundredths, never by moving anything.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: cells filling a grid, both terms of a fraction growing together, a unit fact rewriting an amount, or a used part lifting away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a cell or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a per cent plays in a piece of working: the part the question gives, as shaded cells, a fraction, a decimal or an amount, is deep blue, and the per cent, fraction or decimal the working reaches, with what is left after a part is used, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Both terms multiplied or divided by one number, and the times one hundred step before the % sign, are vermilion. A unit fact that puts two amounts in one unit is violet. The part used, taken away or not won is rose. The step, cell or number being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a decimal is grey. An unshaded cell of a whole stays warm white inside its outline, and the % sign itself is near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Both terms, Unit fact, Used, Not won, Left and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count the shaded parts and all the parts again.
voice.onNext: A new shape. Three names, one amount.
voice.opening: A shape, cut into equal parts, waiting to be named.
voice.onFinish: Every shaded part had three names, and all three agreed.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Shade any shape and read its three names.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has shaded shapes of its own on squared paper and written each shaded part three ways. The tool is what lights the three cards together for one shading and simplifies a fraction while the shading stays still, which paper cannot show happening.

answer_key.rule: Count the shaded parts and the equal parts of the whole, and write the fraction. Grow both terms until the denominator is 100: the hundredths give the decimal, and the number of hundredths is the per cent. All three name one amount. Any equivalent fraction is right unless lowest terms are asked; for lowest terms, divide both terms by their HCF. From a per cent, write it over 100, then simplify. 0.3 and 0.30 are both right. Per cent means out of a hundred. A percentage is an amount written as a per cent. Equivalent fractions name the same amount.
answer_key.wrong: The shape is shown again with the child's shading and the child's card beside a second copy of the shape shaded to the child's answer, so the two amounts are seen side by side, and the card that parts from the others is lit amber. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Count the parts: 11 shaded out of 20 equal parts, so the fraction is 11/20.
20 x 5 = 100, so grow both terms by 5: 11/20 = 55/100.
55/100 is 55 hundredths, so the decimal is 0.55.
55 hundredths is 55%, so all three name one amount.
items.question: A circle is cut into 20 equal parts, and 11 are shaded. Write the shaded part as a fraction, a decimal and a per cent.
items.checkpoint: A fraction, a decimal and a per cent can name one amount.
items.misconception: Writing 11/9, the shaded parts over the unshaded parts instead of over all 20.

steps: 22 of the 50 cells are shaded, so 22/50 names the shaded part.
The HCF of 22 and 50 is 2, and 22/50 = 11/25 in lowest terms.
Both fractions name the same shading, so both are right.
Either way, 22/50 = 44/100, so the decimal is 0.44 and the per cent is 44%.
items.answer: Both. 22/50 = 11/25, so each is right unless lowest terms are asked
items.question: A bar of 50 equal cells has 22 shaded. Is the shaded part 22/50 or 11/25?
items.checkpoint: Any equivalent fraction is right unless lowest terms are asked.
items.misconception: Calling 22/50 wrong because it is not in lowest terms, when the question did not ask for them.

steps: The HCF of 45 and 100 is 5, so 45/100 = 9/20 in lowest terms.
45/100 is 45 hundredths, so the decimal is 0.45.
items.question: A field is 45% sown. What fraction in lowest terms, and what decimal, is sown?
items.checkpoint: Write the per cent over 100, then divide both terms by their HCF.
items.misconception: Writing 45/10 or 4.5, which reads 45% as tenths instead of hundredths.

steps: Per cent means out of a hundred.
So 37% means 37 out of every 100, which is 37/100.
A percentage is an amount written as a per cent, so 37% is a percentage.
items.answer: 37 out of every hundred, which is 37/100. Yes, it is a percentage
items.question: What does 37% mean, and is 37% a percentage?
items.checkpoint: Per cent means out of a hundred, and a percentage is an amount written as a per cent.
items.misconception: Reading 37% as the whole number 37, which leaves out the out of a hundred.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A bar of 2 equal cells has 1 shaded. Write the shaded part as a fraction, a decimal and a per cent.
A bar of 20 equal cells has 18 shaded. Write the shaded part as a fraction in lowest terms.
items.final_answer: 9/10. The HCF of 18 and 20 is 2, and 18/20 = 9/10

items.question: Write 8% as a fraction in lowest terms and as a decimal.
Which of these is a percentage: 0.9, 9/10 or 90%?
items.final_answer: 90%, the amount written as a per cent. All three name one amount

items.question: A square is cut into 25 equal small squares, and 9 are shaded. Write the shaded part as a fraction, a decimal and a per cent.
A circle is cut into 50 equal parts, and 15 are shaded. Write the shaded part two ways as a fraction.
items.final_answer: Such as 15/50 and 3/10, since 15/50 = 3/10. Either is right

items.question: A garden is 64% planted. Write the planted part as a fraction in lowest terms and as a decimal.
Write two fractions equivalent to 3/10, and say what equivalent fractions are.
items.final_answer: Such as 6/20 and 30/100. Equivalent fractions name the same amount

practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: picks a bar of cells, a circle or a square of small squares
cut the shape into 2, 4, 5, 10, 20, 25 or 50 equal parts
shades a part deep blue, or clears it when tapped again
grows both terms until the denominator is 100
divides both terms by their HCF, the shading unchanged
are dragged onto pictures of per cent, percentage and equivalent fractions
are ticked Yes, Almost or Not sure by the child
types a fraction, a decimal or a per cent

teaching_notes: Shade shapes on squared paper before the tool opens, cut into two, four, five, ten, twenty or twenty-five equal parts. Name every shaded part three ways and check all three through hundredths. Accept any equivalent fraction unless lowest terms are asked, and 0.3 or 0.30 alike. Ask for a picture beside each word: a hundred grid for per cent, two equal bars shaded alike for equivalent fractions. The can-do list is the child's own, ticked honestly. Use fresh shapes: the closing page's shapes are the child's to work.
generation_prompt: Build a three names tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A shape at the left, labelled Whole and 100%, is a bar of cells, a circle or a square of small squares, picked on a Shape switch, and Parts buttons cut it into 2, 4, 5, 10, 20, 25 or 50 equal parts. Tapping a part shades it deep blue. Three cards at the right read Fraction, Decimal and Per cent. A Hundredths button grows both terms until the denominator is 100, lighting the words Both terms vermilion, and fills the decimal and per cent cards from the hundredths. A Simplify button divides both terms by their HCF while the shading stays still. The three cards turn green together when they name the shaded part. Typing a per cent shades that many hundredths. On the last phase word cards are dragged onto pictures and can-do cards are ticked Yes, Almost or Not sure. A number pad types fractions, decimals and per cents. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the parts shaded out of the parts. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Shade the shape. Name the shaded part as a fraction, a decimal and a per cent, and check that all three are one amount.
